rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who reject the signs fail to hear, see, and understand, as the Qur’an also says at 7:179.
rows.anchor: they have ears but they hear not and they have eyes but they see not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh should reflect on nearby ruined cities they passed during trade journeys, even if the account of ‘Ād seems remote.
rows.anchor: the demolished and wrecked cities which the Quraysh had the opportunity to pass by in their trade journeys

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God showed the nearby peoples signs in varied ways to turn them to their Creator, but they rejected the signs and were destroyed.
rows.anchor: God’s signs were presented to them in various styles and forms so that they turn to their real Creator and Master

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh are asked why the earlier peoples’ deities failed to save them; those peoples also sought them as intermediaries for nearness to God.
rows.anchor: at the very moment when their help was needed, they were lost to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idolaters invented deities from their fancies, then falsely claimed they were God’s favourites and partners.
rows.anchor: They regarded them to be deities from their own fancies and then falsely ascribed them to be God’s favourites

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word Û is a causative object, expressing the idolaters’ claimed aim of drawing nearer to God through worship.
rows.anchor: The word Û is a causative object (maf‘ūl lahū).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idolaters worshipped these beings as God’s favourites whose worship brought them closer, not as creators and masters; the work discusses this belief about angels elsewhere.
rows.anchor: they worshipped them because they thought that they were God’s favourites

none: bare sūrah heading and title page

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh’s pride in their power is baseless: God destroyed stronger nations, and justice and wisdom require different fates for the rationally guided and desire-led—Paradise for the former, Hell for the latter.
rows.anchor: The pride and conceit which the Quraysh have on their power and might is totally baseless.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 16–19 shift to hypocrites as the Muslims’ hidden enemy: they hear the Prophet but understand nothing, and what strengthens believers’ faith strengthens their hypocrisy.
rows.anchor: These people do apparently listen to what the Prophet (sws) says but understand nothing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites await Judgment though the Messenger’s advent has fulfilled its portents; if it comes suddenly, they will have no time to benefit from God’s counsel.
rows.anchor: after the coming of the Messenger its conditions have been fulfilled.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is directed to seek forgiveness for himself and his companions because punishment may be near.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is directed to seek God’s forgiveness for himself and his companions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 20–31 expose hypocrites who eagerly demanded jihad but became deathly fearful when it was commanded, having only talked bravely.
rows.anchor: initially, they enthusiastically demanded why the directive of jihād is not given to them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites have turned from religion and colluded with Islam’s enemies, promising to support them; God knows their conspiracies.
rows.anchor: These people have in fact turned away from religion and have connived with the enemies of Islam.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though God could expose hypocrites by marking their foreheads, He grants respite and tests them so their concealed evils become evident.
rows.anchor: If He wanted, He could have asked their foreheads to bear witness against them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion returns to the sūrah’s opening: Muslims, especially hypocrites, must obey every directive of God and His Messenger or their deeds will bear no fruit.
rows.anchor: This is the concluding part of the sūrah in which the subject with which it began is reminded of.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers have no strength, so compromising with them relies on a frail shelter; Muslims should strive confidently, knowing God is with them.
rows.anchor: those who are trying to compromise with them are seeking refuge in a frail shelter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims should not let worldly pleasures deter them from spending for God; this is profitable, and God rewards every penny.
rows.anchor: God will reward each and every penny they spend.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section on verses 16–38 continues the sūrah’s hypocrite theme; a major campaign makes it essential to expose hidden Muslims whose weakness and collusion threaten the community.
rows.anchor: When Muslims were asked to undertake a big campaign, it became essential that a group lurking among them as their hidden enemy be exposed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says the Qur’an discusses hypocrites in the same manner in al-Nisāʾ, al-Māʾidah, al-Anfāl, al-Tawbah, and other sūrahs.
rows.anchor: They are mentioned here with the same reference as they are mentioned in S ūrah al-Nisā’, S ūrah al-Mā’idah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first section depicts listeners who understand nothing and await punishment’s sign, unaware that a messenger’s advent already portends punishment for unbelievers.
rows.anchor: there is a group among the Muslims who does listen to what he says, yet understands nothing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second section exposes hypocrites who profess zeal for jihad but fear death when ordered, turn from religion, and associate with God’s enemies; trials will expose their weakness.
rows.anchor: they zealously express from their tongues their readiness for jihād

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final section recalls the sūrah’s opening: Muslims should struggle for religion’s supremacy instead of compromising with the doomed; if worldliness makes them turn away, God will replace them with better people.
rows.anchor: instead of thinking of ways and means to strike a compromise with them, they should get ready to struggle for the supremacy of religion.
